title: Put Saving on the Payday Clock
meta_description: Build a payday-based saving system that fits real bills, variable income, debt and quarterly reviews without causing overdrafts or reversals.

sections.heading: Your Paycheck Arrives With Competition
paragraphs: Most saving failures do not begin with a conscious decision to abandon the future. They begin when income lands in an account already surrounded by claims. Rent, groceries, loan payments, subscriptions, family requests and ordinary pleasures all compete with a transfer that has no immediate consequence if it is postponed. Waiting to save whatever remains at the end of the month gives every other expense the first move. By the time a good mood and an uncluttered balance coincide, the money may have acquired another job.

Calendar-based saving changes the order rather than demanding constant enthusiasm. A transfer tied to payday makes saving one of the first claims on income. The decision is made when the plan is calm, then executed when cash is actually available. This is not proof that motivation is irrelevant. Motivation chooses the destination, amount and trade-offs. The calendar prevents that choice from being reopened after every advertisement, difficult day or unusually expensive weekend.

The distinction matters because automation is often marketed as a cure for undisciplined people. That framing is both insulting and incomplete. A reliable transfer can fail when its date conflicts with rent, when an employer pays late, when variable income falls, or when the checking account has no operating cushion. An automated mistake is still a mistake; it merely repeats without requiring attention. The useful habit is therefore not 'set it and forget it.' It is set it deliberately, observe it, and revise it when the cash-flow system changes.

The national backdrop shows why a modest buffer deserves priority. The Federal Reserve reported that 63 percent of adults in 2024 would cover a $400 emergency expense using cash or its equivalent, while 55 percent said they had savings sufficient for three months of expenses. [[S3|Those household measures]] describe broad financial resilience, not a prescription for every reader, but they show that many households remain exposed to relatively ordinary disruptions. A scheduled transfer cannot solve low wages, medical costs or unstable work. It can stop available surplus from being assigned accidentally to lower priorities.

Treat the calendar as financial infrastructure. Good infrastructure routes cash predictably while leaving room for exceptions. This article builds that route from the timing of real pay and bills, distinguishes dependable transfers from clever spending triggers, and shows how to handle raises, irregular income, debt and reviews. The goal is not the largest transfer a spreadsheet can tolerate in an average month. It is the strongest transfer that can survive an inconvenient month without causing an overdraft, a credit-card rebound or a panicked cancellation.

A calendar also removes a common accounting illusion: treating whatever appears in checking as available to spend. Once future bills and a planned transfer are visible on dates, today's displayed balance stops pretending to be discretionary cash. That visibility can improve decisions even before the first transfer runs. It shows which weeks are crowded, which expenses deserve a sinking fund, and whether the plan depends on income arriving with impossible precision.

sections.heading: What the Evidence Says—and Does Not Say
paragraphs: Automatic saving has an intuitive advantage: it converts an intention into a default action. Evidence supports that mechanism, but not the exaggerated claim that defaults make outcomes effortless or uniform. A Department of Labor evidence review of three companies found that automatic enrollment increased retirement-plan participation and produced striking clustering at default contribution rates. The share contributing at the default rose from 21 to 57 percent at one company, from 7 to 72 percent at another, and from 12 to 46 percent at the third. Yet [[S4|the review rated the causal evidence low]], an important limitation when translating workplace findings into universal advice.

Defaults can help people begin, but the chosen default can also become an anchor. The Government Accountability Office found that automatic enrollment showed promise while warning that low initial contribution rates and incomplete escalation could suppress adequate long-term accumulation. [[S5|The GAO analysis]] is a useful corrective to celebratory automation stories: high participation at an inadequate rate is not the same as a well-funded plan. A system should make the right action easy without disguising whether the amount is sufficient for the actual goal.

More recent research also counsels modest expectations. A 2024 National Bureau of Economic Research working paper accounted for worker opt-outs and saving that may be displaced elsewhere. Its estimated steady-state effects were about 0.6 percent of income for automatic enrollment and 0.3 percent for default auto-escalation. [[S6|The paper's estimates]] do not mean defaults are pointless. Small recurring changes can matter over long periods. They mean that gross contribution changes should not automatically be treated as equally large increases in total household wealth.

Emergency-saving evidence points in the same practical direction. A CFPB analysis of users of a savings app found that guaranteed rules—such as payday or recurring transfers—were associated with roughly 1.5 to 3.5 times larger increases in maximum savings and the likelihood of reaching savings milestones than contingent rules linked to spending behavior. [[S2|The CFPB report]] describes associations in a specific user population, not randomized proof that the rule alone caused the difference. Even so, it supports a sensible design preference: when income timing is known, transfer a defined amount rather than hoping a purchase-triggered trick will do the work.

The honest conclusion is narrower and more useful than 'automation works.' Defaults reduce repeated decisions and may raise participation or accumulation. Results depend on the amount, timing, opt-outs, competing debts and what would have happened otherwise. The calendar should carry an already reasoned plan; it cannot reason on the household's behalf. Measure success by the growth of usable reserves and progress toward named goals, not by the mere presence of an automatic-transfer icon in a banking app.

Evidence should change the design, not decorate it. The findings favor simple defaults while also revealing default dependence and offsetting behavior. That combination argues for a system that starts automatically but reports its result plainly. Participation, gross contributions and app milestones are intermediate measures. The household outcome is stronger only when liquid reserves, debt-adjusted wealth or funded long-term goals improve without hidden damage elsewhere in the balance sheet.

sections.heading: Draw a Payday Map Before Moving Money
paragraphs: Do not begin by choosing a percentage. Begin with dates. Take the last two or three months of checking activity and mark every dependable inflow: salary deposits, benefits, support payments and predictable business draws. Then mark required outflows by due date, including bills that arrive quarterly or annually. A monthly budget can look comfortably positive while a checking account runs short on the twelfth because most obligations cluster before the second paycheck. Automation must fit the sequence of cash, not only the monthly total.

Build a simple payday map with four columns: date, expected inflow, required outflow and lowest projected balance. Include a conservative allowance for food, transport and other essential variable spending between deposits. For annual insurance, school fees, taxes or maintenance, divide the expected amount by the number of pay periods remaining and treat that sinking-fund contribution as a current claim. This prevents a predictable bill from masquerading as an emergency when it arrives.

Next identify the safe window. For a stable employee paid every other Friday, that may be the morning after each deposit clears. Scheduling on payday itself can work, but a one-day gap gives the account time to show whether payroll was delayed or reduced. For someone paid on the first and fifteenth, the two transfers need not be equal if rent dominates the first half of the month. Matching the transfer to each pay cycle is more robust than forcing a visually tidy monthly amount.

Keep an operating floor in checking. This is not the emergency fund; it is a small timing cushion that protects routine automation from weekends, bank holds, bill changes and minor estimation errors. Choose the floor from observed volatility rather than a generic rule. A household with synchronized salary and predictable bills may need less than a contractor whose clients pay several days late. If a proposed transfer pushes the projected balance below that floor, reduce it or move the date.

A map also exposes false surplus. Credit-card purchases may leave checking cash apparently untouched until the statement is due. A reimbursement may look like income even though it repays an expense already charged. A tax refund or bonus is real cash but not necessarily repeatable pay. Label these separately. The recurring transfer should be supported by recurring free cash flow; one-time inflows can receive their own decision rule. [[I1|Daily Yield's calculators]] can help test amounts, but the bank statement supplies the dates that make the plan executable.

When mapping couples' or families' cash flow, agree which account carries each obligation. Two incomes do not automatically create one synchronized payday, and duplicated assumptions can leave both people believing the other account will cover a bill. A shared calendar can show amounts without requiring every purchase to be policed. The objective is operational clarity: one owner, one funding account and one expected date for each material claim.

sections.heading: Choose a Transfer That Can Survive
paragraphs: The first amount should be meaningful enough to build evidence of progress and small enough to repeat through an ordinary bad month. Start with actual free cash flow after essential bills, minimum debt payments, predictable irregular expenses and the checking floor. If that number varies, use the lower end of recent normal months rather than the average. An average is easily inflated by one unusually cheap month and can turn automation into a recurring cash shortage.

A useful calibration method has three levels. The base transfer is the amount that should run after nearly every normal paycheck. A sweep is an optional additional transfer made after the next payday once the prior period's bills have cleared. A windfall rule assigns a stated share of bonuses, refunds or gifts. Separating these levels avoids the false choice between timid automation and an aggressive fixed amount. The dependable base creates continuity; the flexible layers capture upside without promising that upside will recur.

Choose the destination according to purpose. Near-term emergency money belongs in an accessible, appropriately insured deposit account rather than an asset whose value can fall when cash is needed. A known bill due within months may need its own labeled sinking fund. Long-term retirement contributions can use workplace payroll deductions or an investment account suited to the goal and tax situation. Do not send every dollar to the highest-yielding destination if doing so leaves checking fragile or forces expensive borrowing.

Run a two-cycle test before increasing the amount. Observe whether bills clear without transfers back from savings, new revolving debt or anxiety-driven cancellations. A transfer that repeatedly reverses is not evidence of weak character; it is feedback that the amount, date or budget assumptions are wrong. Reduce or reschedule it, then test again. The durable habit is net saving—the amount that remains saved after withdrawals and debt rebound—not the impressive gross total shown in transfer history.

Give the transfer a name tied to a function: 'one-month buffer,' 'car insurance in November,' or 'retirement contribution.' Specificity makes trade-offs visible. Research on savings goals has found that concentrating attention on one integrated goal can improve implementation compared with juggling several competing goals. That does not require one account forever. It suggests that early automation should have a clear priority rather than scattering tiny amounts across so many labels that none reaches a useful threshold.

Do not let a percentage obscure the dollar consequence. Ten percent may be easy for one paycheck and destabilizing for another household with the same income but different fixed obligations. Write both figures and project the post-transfer balance. If the amount feels surprisingly high or trivial, investigate why. The exercise can reveal that the real constraint is a recurring commitment, irregular bill or underestimated category rather than the saving goal itself.

sections.heading: Prefer Guaranteed Rules to Spending Tricks
paragraphs: Not every automated rule is equally dependable. A guaranteed rule moves a fixed dollar amount or percentage when an identifiable event occurs, usually a paycheck. A contingent rule reacts to behavior: rounding purchases, transferring after a card swipe, or saving when a particular product is not bought. Contingent rules can make saving engaging, but their output depends on spending. A quiet spending week may produce less saving; heavy spending may trigger more transfers precisely when the checking account is under pressure.

Roundups illustrate the confusion. Moving the difference between a purchase and the next dollar can accumulate small amounts, yet the mechanism still begins with consumption. It may supplement a payday transfer, but it should not persuade someone that more purchases create financial progress. The CFPB app study's association between guaranteed rules and stronger accumulation offers a reason to put the reliable rule first. Use a spending-linked feature only after understanding its cash-flow effect and fees.

Bank features deserve scrutiny. Check whether failed transfers create overdraft charges, whether the savings account limits withdrawals, how long transfers remain pending, and whether balances earn a competitive rate without monthly fees. Read what happens when the scheduled date falls on a weekend or holiday. If checking and savings are at different institutions, allow for settlement time. Convenience does not eliminate account terms, and a glossy app interface does not establish deposit insurance or fiduciary responsibility.

Split direct deposit is often cleaner because saving occurs before money reaches the everyday account. [[S1|The CFPB's emergency-fund guidance]] identifies recurring bank transfers and split direct deposit as practical options. Availability depends on the employer and payroll system, and the amount still needs review. If pay changes, an exact-dollar split may become too large or too small. If the emergency account is already funded, the split should be redirected to the next priority rather than continuing by inertia.

Keep rules legible. You should be able to state what triggers each transfer, its maximum amount, destination, purpose and cancellation method. Multiple overlapping apps can create invisible claims against the same balance and make troubleshooting difficult. One dependable payday rule plus a clearly defined windfall rule is often stronger than a web of gamified triggers. Complexity earns its place only when it solves a real timing problem and can be audited from statements.

Gamification can be useful when it keeps attention on a goal, but it should never make the rule difficult to explain or leave the user uncertain about tomorrow's balance. Treat rewards, streaks and celebratory notifications as interface features, not financial evidence. The durable record is the statement: money arrived, required claims cleared, the transfer remained saved, and no avoidable fee or expensive balance appeared because of it.

sections.heading: Escalate With Raises, Not Wishful Forecasts
paragraphs: A transfer that never grows can become too small as income rises and goals change. Automatic escalation addresses that drift by scheduling a future increase, commonly after a raise or once a debt payment ends. The behavioral advantage is advance commitment: tomorrow's higher income has not yet been absorbed into recurring spending. The well-known Save More Tomorrow program asked workers to commit a share of future raises; average saving rates among participants in its first implementation rose from 3.5 percent to 13.6 percent over 40 months. [[S7|The published study]] is influential, but its setting and participant choices should not be mistaken for a guaranteed household result.

Tie escalation to an observable event. Examples include increasing a workplace contribution by one percentage point after an annual raise, redirecting half of a finished loan payment, or adding a fixed amount after childcare costs fall. Avoid escalating merely because a calendar year changed if income did not. A planned increase without supporting cash flow may be funded through reduced liquidity or credit-card debt, leaving the household worse off despite a higher displayed contribution rate.

Retirement defaults require special attention. Enrolling automatically at a low rate may be better than not enrolling, especially when an employer match is available, but the default is not a recommendation tailored to age, income or retirement goals. Review the contribution rate, investment selection, vesting rules, match formula and fees. Increasing contributions while carrying costly revolving debt may or may not be the best next dollar; compare the certain interest cost, lost match and need for emergency liquidity rather than repeating slogans.

Set a ceiling and review point for escalation. A plan might increase by one percentage point after each raise until a chosen rate is reached, subject to a cash-flow check. The ceiling is not permanent proof of adequacy; it prevents an unattended rule from crowding out near-term obligations. Major changes—home purchase, caregiving, unpaid leave, marriage or a move—should interrupt the schedule for reassessment.

Protect at least part of every improvement in cash flow before lifestyle commitments expand to absorb it. That principle works beyond salary. When an insurance premium falls, a subscription is canceled or a tax installment ends, decide in advance where the released amount goes. Some can support current life; some can strengthen reserves or long-term saving. Automation is most powerful at these transition points because it captures money before it becomes psychologically ordinary.

Inflation and taxes can change the appropriate escalation path. A nominal raise may mainly preserve purchasing power, while a promotion can create genuine additional capacity. Compare the after-tax change in take-home pay with rising essential costs before committing all of it. Even when the full increase cannot be saved, directing a deliberate portion preserves progress and prevents every improvement from disappearing into unexamined recurring spending.

sections.heading: Build a Different Clock for Uneven Income
paragraphs: Freelancers, commission workers, seasonal employees and small-business owners cannot safely copy a fixed payday design built for identical checks. Their calendar still matters, but the trigger should be cleared income rather than an assumed date. Start by separating business receipts, taxes, business expenses and personal pay. Revenue is not the same as spendable household income. Transferring savings from gross receipts before reserving taxes and operating costs can manufacture a crisis later.

Create an income floor from conservative history. Review at least a year if the work is seasonal, and identify the amount that arrived in weaker ordinary months. Base fixed personal commitments on that floor when possible. Then use a percentage waterfall each time a client payment clears: reserve taxes, replenish essential business costs, pay a stable personal draw, fund the operating buffer, and direct an agreed share of excess toward savings or debt. Percentages can adapt better than a fixed dollar transfer, but they still need minimum cash reserves and caps.

Maintain separate buffers for different risks. A business operating reserve covers delayed invoices or necessary equipment. A personal emergency fund covers household disruption. A tax reserve holds money that was never available for consumption. Combining all three in one impressive balance invites double counting. Clear labels or separate accounts make the purpose visible, provided fees and account complexity remain reasonable.

Schedule a monthly reconciliation even when transfers occur per payment. Confirm which invoices are still outstanding, what taxes are due, whether business spending was properly recorded, and how much can safely become personal savings. In a strong month, resist raising the permanent transfer immediately. First repair buffers depleted during weaker periods and provision known annual costs. In a weak month, pause the optional sweep before raiding tax money or using expensive credit.

Households with one stable income and one variable income can use a hybrid. Let dependable pay cover as much of the essential baseline as practical and support a modest fixed transfer. Apply a waterfall to the variable income for taxes, catch-up saving, debt reduction and discretionary goals. This design makes progress during good periods without requiring every commission check to rescue a budget built around best-case earnings. The calendar becomes a set of conditional gates, not a fiction that uneven money arrives evenly.

Variable-income plans also need a rule for exceptionally large receipts. Before treating one contract or commission as a new normal, reserve the taxes and costs attached to it, rebuild any depleted buffers, and look at the pipeline for the next several months. Only then divide the remainder among long-term goals and current enjoyment. This sequence permits celebration without converting a temporary peak into permanent monthly obligations.

sections.heading: Check Debt, Leakage and Account Friction
paragraphs: Saving and borrowing must be reviewed together. A household can transfer money faithfully while an expensive card balance grows because checking is too tight. That is not genuine progress. Track net cash accumulation after new debt, interest and withdrawals. An emergency buffer may justify saving some cash while paying debt, because without liquidity the next repair returns to the card. Beyond that buffer, compare the debt's rate and risk with the purpose and expected return of additional saving.

Look for leakage created by timing. Overdraft fees, late fees, expedited-payment charges and savings transfers reversed to cover bills can consume the benefit of interest earned. Move due dates where creditors permit, align transfers after cleared deposits, and keep alerts for low balances and unusually large transactions. Alerts are not a substitute for reserves; they are an early-warning layer that gives you time to pause an optional transfer.

Account friction can either protect or obstruct. Keeping emergency savings at a separate institution may reduce casual spending, but transfer delays matter in a true emergency. A savings account linked instantly to checking is convenient but easy to raid. Choose enough friction to preserve the goal without blocking legitimate access. Test the withdrawal process before relying on it, verify deposit-insurance coverage and keep beneficiary information current where applicable.

Audit subscriptions and recurring bills on the same schedule as saving automation. The calendar should not privilege every old merchant charge while forcing the newest goal to absorb all adjustment. Cancel what no longer provides value, renegotiate material services, and redirect at least part of the released cash. Focus first on recurring commitments large enough to change the plan; minor cuts cannot compensate indefinitely for unaffordable housing, transportation or high-interest financing.

Security belongs in the system. Use multifactor authentication, unique passwords and transaction alerts. Confirm transfer instructions through the bank's official app or website rather than links in messages. Review authorized third-party apps and revoke access that is no longer needed. Automation increases the number of unattended movements, so statements still require human inspection. A fraudulent charge or duplicated rule left unnoticed for months can undo more than a small interest-rate improvement will earn.

If debt is consolidated or refinanced, do not count a lower required payment as savings until the old account is closed or controlled and the released cash has a destination. Otherwise the household may regain borrowing capacity while keeping the same spending pattern. Schedule the redirected amount alongside the new payment from the first cycle. Then verify that total interest, fees and payoff time actually improve rather than relying on a smaller monthly bill alone.

sections.heading: The Quarterly Reset Keeps the Clock Honest
paragraphs: A quarterly review is frequent enough to catch drift and infrequent enough to avoid reacting to every unusual grocery week. Put the review on the calendar when the transfer is created. Gather the previous three months of bank, credit-card and loan statements. Record gross transfers into savings, withdrawals back out, new debt, interest paid and the ending balances for each named goal. The central number is net progress, not activity.

Ask five questions. Did every transfer occur after income cleared? Did checking remain above its operating floor? Were any transfers reversed or indirectly financed by a card? Has the purpose or target amount changed? Is the next quarter likely to contain irregular bills, travel, leave or income disruption? Each answer should produce a specific adjustment, not a vague promise to be more careful.

Use a simple status system. Keep a rule that ran cleanly and remains aligned with its goal. Resize a rule when the amount is consistently too easy or repeatedly strains cash flow. Reschedule when the amount is sound but the date collides with bills. Redirect when a goal is completed. Pause when income becomes uncertain, while preserving the review date so a temporary stop does not become permanent neglect. Delete duplicate or obsolete triggers rather than leaving them dormant and confusing.

Review progress in units connected to life: weeks of essential expenses, the percentage of an annual insurance bill funded, the remaining high-cost debt balance, or the contribution rate toward retirement. Bank balances alone can be misleading when several purposes share one account. At least once a year, revisit the larger plan, including insurance, taxes, beneficiaries, employer benefits and whether the emergency target still reflects household risks.

The calendar is successful when it makes good behavior ordinary without making attention disappear. A strong system does not demand a burst of willpower every payday, and it does not continue blindly through changed circumstances. It routes a conservative amount, protects the operating account, captures part of future improvements and asks for deliberate review. Put saving on the payday clock—but keep a human hand on the clock's settings.

Keep a short change log beside the quarterly review: what changed, why, who approved it and when it will be reconsidered. This prevents future confusion about whether a paused transfer was intentional or forgotten. It also makes the system easier to maintain during stressful events, when reconstructing old reasoning is difficult. Good automation leaves an audit trail that another responsible adult in the household can understand.

summary: Calendar-based saving solves a sequencing problem: when saving waits until the end of the month, every other claim on income moves first. A transfer tied to cleared pay gives a chosen goal an earlier place in the cash-flow order. It does not replace motivation or repair inadequate income. It carries out a decision repeatedly so that the decision does not have to compete with mood, advertising and daily spending after every paycheck.

Evidence supports a measured case for automation. Workplace automatic enrollment can raise participation and cause workers to cluster at default contribution rates, but the Department of Labor rated the causal evidence from a prominent three-company study low. GAO has warned that low defaults and incomplete escalation can leave people contributing too little. A 2024 NBER working paper estimated smaller steady-state effects after accounting for opt-outs and offsets: about 0.6 percent of income for automatic enrollment and 0.3 percent for default escalation.

For short-term saving, a CFPB study of savings-app users found that guaranteed payday or recurring rules were associated with roughly 1.5 to 3.5 times larger increases in maximum savings and milestone achievement than contingent rules. The study was observational, so it does not prove the rules caused the outcomes. It nevertheless supports putting a dependable income-linked transfer ahead of roundups and spending-triggered gimmicks.

Design starts with a payday map, not a generic percentage. Mark when dependable income clears, when required bills leave, and the lowest projected checking balance in each pay period. Provision annual and quarterly costs through sinking funds. Keep a checking operating floor for ordinary timing errors. Schedule the transfer after cleared income and adapt unequal pay cycles rather than forcing one tidy monthly amount.

Calibrate a base transfer from conservative free cash flow. Add optional layers: a sweep after bills clear and a separate rule for windfalls. Test the base across two pay cycles and measure net saving after withdrawals and new card debt. Repeated reversals are evidence that the amount or date needs repair, not that the household should hide the problem behind a more ambitious rule.

Escalation works best when tied to real improvements such as a raise, completed loan or lower childcare expense. Decide in advance what share will be redirected, but review the change before it runs. A retirement-plan default is a starting setting, not personalized advice. Check the contribution, employer match, investments, fees and competing high-cost debt rather than assuming automatic enrollment guarantees adequacy.

Uneven income needs a different clock. Trigger a percentage waterfall only after client or commission income clears. Reserve taxes and business costs, support a stable personal draw, replenish operating and personal buffers, then assign excess to saving or debt. Keep tax, business and household reserves conceptually separate so one balance is not promised to three risks.

Finally, review the machinery quarterly. Compare gross transfers with withdrawals, new debt, fees and ending goal balances. Keep, resize, reschedule, redirect, pause or delete each rule. Check security and third-party access as well as account terms. The aim is not to forget money forever. It is to make a conservative good action routine while preserving scheduled moments for human judgment.

A successful system is deliberately boring. It makes the transfer after dependable cash arrives, protects a realistic operating floor, and records enough detail to reveal whether the money stayed saved. It also anticipates transitions: raises, completed debts, irregular invoices and finished goals. The calendar reduces repeated choice, but the quarterly reset supplies accountability. Together they create a habit that can survive ordinary setbacks without confusing automation with certainty or treating a default amount as permanent financial advice.

faq.question: Should an automatic transfer run on payday?
faq.answer: Usually schedule it after the deposit has cleared, especially if payroll timing can vary. A one-day gap can reduce the risk of transferring against a late or smaller check.

faq.question: How much should I automate first?
faq.answer: Use conservative recurring free cash flow after essential bills, debt minimums, irregular-expense provisions and a checking operating floor. Test the amount for two pay cycles before increasing it.

faq.question: Are roundups enough for an emergency fund?
faq.answer: Roundups can supplement saving, but their output depends on spending. A defined payday or recurring transfer is easier to forecast and should generally carry the core plan.

faq.question: What if my income changes every month?
faq.answer: Trigger a percentage waterfall after income clears. Reserve taxes and business costs first, support a stable personal draw and buffers, then allocate excess to savings or debt.

faq.question: Should I save while paying credit-card debt?
faq.answer: A modest emergency buffer can reduce the chance of new borrowing. Beyond that, compare the debt rate, employer match, liquidity needs and risks; track saving net of new debt and interest.

faq.question: How often should I review automatic saving?
faq.answer: Quarterly is practical for many households, with immediate review after a job change, leave, major purchase, new dependent or other material cash-flow shift.

glossary.definition: A bank instruction that moves money on a schedule or after a defined event.
A payroll arrangement sending portions of pay directly to two or more accounts.
The minimum checking balance retained to absorb routine timing variation and small errors.
Money accumulated gradually for a known irregular expense.
A savings rule that transfers a defined amount or percentage after a predictable event such as pay.
A transfer triggered by behavior or conditions, such as purchase roundups.
A scheduled future increase in a contribution rate or amount.
An ordered allocation of each receipt among taxes, costs, reserves, goals and spending.
The amount that remains accumulated after withdrawals, reversals and related new debt.
The tendency for participation or choices to be influenced by a preselected setting.
